method: Questions were researched with an evidence-only retrieval tool over one corpus of open-access and public-domain texts (see corpus.json). Each excerpt was checked word for word against the corpus passage it cites when this file was written; corpus_chunk numbers that passage in the corpus snapshot of 2026-10-01.
questions: What did Hume say about is and ought, and how has it been interpreted?
What is Hume's law, and why is the gap thought to exist?
Do thick concepts bridge the gap?

evidence.excerpt: at some point make an unremarked transition from premises whose parts are linked only by “is” to conclusions whose parts are linked by “ought”
Few passages in Hume’s work have generated more interpretive controversy.
that no ethical or indeed evaluative conclusion whatsoever may be validly inferred from any set of purely factual premises
A number of present-day philosophers, including R. M. Hare, endorse this putative thesis of logic, calling it “Hume’s Law.”
on this reading Hume must simply assume that no purely factual propositions are themselves evaluative, as he does not argue for this
Some interpreters think Hume commits himself here to a non-propositional or noncognitivist view of moral judgment
which must involve the use of sentiment
he or she may reach some particular moral conclusions by inference from causal, factual premises
They point out that Hume himself makes such inferences frequently in his writings.
Any (non-trivial) valid argument for an evaluative conclusion must somehow (perhaps implicitly) involve evaluative content in its premises.
evaluative and normative statements commend things and guide action, whereas purely non-evaluative statements play no such practical role by themselves
note that an important gap can be held to exist even if values are a special kind of facts
But that debate concerns moral metaphysics rather than thick concepts.
O: x causes offense by indicating lack of respect So, R: x is rude
O*: x is an overt sexual display So, L: x is lewd
